findings.statement: The authors were unable to replicate the reported improvement of SIGN over GCN.
findings.quote: On the other hand, the authors of SIGN  report an improvement over GCN , which we were not able to replicate in our experiments.
findings.label: Reproduction report

findings.statement: Existing attacks use a validation set much larger than the training set and assume it is clean, which is unrealistic.
findings.quote: All existing label poisoning attacks (LPATTACK, LAFAK, MG) evaluate on data splits with validation (val) set size much larger than that of training (train) set. To substantiate, in the default setting as tabulated in Table 1 in the Appendix, the val set contains 500 nodes and the train set contains 20 nodes per class (e.g. 140 nodes in the Cora-ML dataset). Moreover, the labels of the validation set are assumed to be clean – not poisoned.
findings.label: Protocol note

findings.topic: Default hyperparameters tuned on clean labels
findings.statement: All label‑poisoning attacks use default hyper‑parameters that were tuned for clean labels, ignoring the effect of poisoning.
findings.quote: Despite establishing this, all the label-poisoning attacks for GNNs still use default h-params to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed attack. The default h-params were tuned to work with clean labels (unpoisoned).
findings.label: Note

findings.statement: Assuming a clean validation set separate from training data is unrealistic because the defender cannot know which labels are corrupted.
findings.quote: It is an unrealistic assumption for an attacker to treat train and val sets as separate entities. In other words, the current evaluation setup in literature for label-poisoning attacks training nodes while the val set is untouched and remains sanitized.
findings.label: Protocol note

items.explanation: The paper evaluates models using many random data splits and multiple initializations, so a reimplementation using a single fixed split could obtain different results.
items.quote: splitting the data in a different way results in a different performance of each method.

items.explanation: The authors report average performance over 2,000 random settings (100 splittings × 20 initializations), which differs from evaluations that use a single train/validation/test split.
items.quote: they introduce 4 new datasets and find the average performance of each one of the methods on 2,000 random settings (100 random splittings of the datasets and for each one of them 20 random initializations of parameters)

items.explanation: The paper states that using the same train/validation/test splits and altering training procedures (e.g., early stopping) prevents fair comparison, and that different splits lead to dramatically different model rankings.
items.quote: We show that using the same train/validation/test splits of the same datasets, as well as making significant changes to the training procedure (e.g. early stopping criteria) precludes a fair comparison of different architectures.

items.topic: hyperparameters that the paper does not state
items.explanation: The paper notes that simpler GNN architectures can outperform more sophisticated ones only if hyperparameters and training procedures are tuned fairly for all models, implying that unstated hyperparameter choices affect results.
items.quote: Even more importantly, our findings suggest that simpler GNN architectures are able to outperform the more sophisticated ones if the hyperparameters and the training procedure are tuned fairly for all models.

items.topic: results that others could not reproduce
items.explanation: By showing that rankings change dramatically across different data splits, the paper indicates that reported numbers may not be reproducible when using alternative splits.
items.quote: We perform a thorough empirical evaluation of four prominent GNN models and show that considering different splits of the data leads to dramatically different rankings of models.
